title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
text: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
author: Basil Chatha
text: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. Jump to the MCP discussion → "Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. title: Issue #238 : Software Testing Notes
author: Pritesh Usadadiya
text: Hello there! 👋 Welcome to the 238th edition of Software Testing Notes , a weekly newsletter featuring must-read content on Software Testing. I hope this week has been good for you so far. Thanks for reading Software Testing Notes! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. AI is changing how quickly we build software, but faster development doesn’t automatically mean better software. From AI-generated tests that confidently miss the wrong behaviour to thousands of passing tests that fail to catch production bugs, this week’s articles explore why we need to rethink how we approach quality. We’re also looking at how QA can get involved earlier, how teams can scale testing without creating bottlenecks, and how to make automation more reliable across APIs, Android apps, and accessibility workflows. Here’s what to expect this week: Scaling testing practices and QA responsibilities in the age of AI. Understanding why green tests don’t always mean correct software. Exploring AI-powered testing agents and more reliable automation strategies. Testing webhook failures, API contracts, and security integrations. Benchmarking vector indexes under realistic workloads. Automating screen reader checks and practical accessibility testing. Let’s get into it! Reach thousands of software testers across our QA ecosystem with a sponsored link → 📚 Testing Thoughts How do we scale testing ? by Melissa Fisher AI is increasing the amount of code teams produce, but testing capacity is not keeping pace. Melissa Fisher explores seven areas that help organisations scale quality alongside development, from building testing skills and shortening feedback cycles to setting clear quality expectations and using AI responsibly. Why QA Should Start Before the First Feature Is Built by Andrii Khomenko Some of the most expensive software defects start as assumptions that nobody questioned during product discovery. Andrii Khomenko explains how QA can work with product, design, and engineering teams before development begins to uncover missing requirements, clarify expected behaviour, and identify risks while they are still inexpensive to address. Green Tests, Wrong Answers by Alan Page What happens when AI writes both the application and the tests that are supposed to verify it? Alan Page examines why matching assumptions can produce green test suites that still miss incorrect behaviour, and explores how independent validation, clear acceptance criteria can help establish whether an application actually works as intended. Tests as data by Martin Fowler When AI agents can freely rewrite both production code and its tests, how do you protect the original requirements? Martin Fowler proposes treating tests as readable, independent data rather than code, exploring tabular scenarios, custom DSLs, and AI-generated test runners that keep behavioural specifications visible and easier for humans to review. Share ⚙️ Automation Testing The Test Suite Is the New Code Review by Allen Hutchison AI coding agents can now produce and review code faster than a large monorepo’s test suite can process it. Allen Hutchison explores how breaking a monorepo into smaller repositories, defining clear interfaces, and coordinating specialised agents can reduce CI bottlenecks and keep development moving. We handed testing to AI. Here is what stayed human. by Roman Nikolaev Roman Nikolaev shares how his team uses Claude Code to handle 75 to 85% of its testing, from analysing tickets to selecting scenarios and executing checks. The interesting part is what remains human: assessing risk, making release decisions, and building the systems that keep AI-driven testing reliable. Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale What if every code change came with AI-generated tests designed to catch bugs before the change reached production? title: Fragments: November 20
author: Martin Fowler (martin@martinfowler.com)
text: Marcus Borg recounts an experiment to investigate if healthy code was cheaper for agents to review . Between a typical unhealthy pull request (CodeHealth 2.8) and a typical healthy one (9.7), that adds up to 22 to 35%. The measures of health come from CodeScene. The experiment looked at three LLMs, 465 pull requests on 246 open source repositories. Each pull request was put through a review and fix pipeline involving five agents. They also looked at which code smells led to increased costs: they highlighted Complex Method and Complex Conditional from the smells identified by CodeScene. Another drop of evidence that good quality code matters in agentic engineering. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Gergely Orosz: One usage for AI: for these 100-page-long terms-and-service agreements you NEED to agree to, to eg play the game / sign up for a $10/month service and can never ever ever read as a regular person: I paste into AI and ask: “anything weird in this?” Before hitting “agree” ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Andrew Sharp has a good analysis of Jensen Huang and the crisis at Nvidia . While he starts off in a key that sounds worryingly like he thinks this is all a nothingburger, he goes on to explain in detail why this affair(s) is a problem at many levels, not just for Huang and Nvida, but also for Silicon Valley and the Trump Administration’s culture of impunity. For as brilliant and charming and tenacious as Jensen Huang may be—and as omnipotent as he may have seemed to people in the tech industry—we should be clear that his fundamental stupidity is not confined to multiple cases of workplace infidelity. Zooming out, this is a man whose technology became economically critical almost overnight, and it thrust him into a role navigating a geopolitical environment he simply could not handle. Huang’s highly centralized management style means that many people are worried about how Nvidia will operate without his hands on every lever. I don’t have any worthwhile insight here, but I am struck when he is compared in this way to Steve Jobs. I’ve always felt that one of the marks of a great leader is whether they can build something that can manage without them. Alexander the Great conquered a massive empire, but once he was dead it quickly withered away. Steve Jobs, for all his control of Apple, built a company that has done very well in the decade and a half since he left us. When we think of his achievements, the fact that he put together the people, organization, and culture to do this is one of the highlights of his ability. If Huang is to be compared to Jobs, what happens to Nvidia next will be part of the assessment. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Steve Yegge tells everyone to slow down with software factories If you don’t pace your AI to human speeds, everything starts breaking around you, even at small operations like my online video game. I only have about a dozen humans working with my factory, and only a few hundred active old-timer players in the community who get along well, and still, introducing AI has still been very rocky. I hear a lot about how agents go so fast that humans can’t keep up, and are thus tempted to lose visibility to what the agents are doing. That’s opening ourselves to a whole lot of risk. There’s an argument for keeping the agents to a human-governable speed, one that may increase as humans learn to govern agents more effectively, but should still be limited by those the agents are supposed to serve. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ This post on the future of SaaS from Chad Fowler (no relation) is pretty compelling Companies will still pay other companies to host important software, secure it, operate it, maintain authoritative data, track regulatory changes, connect to external networks, and answer the phone when something breaks. What is much less obviously going to survive is the assumption that ten thousand different companies should use substantially the same application. title: Za nami Infoshare Katowice 2026. Technologie, biznes i przyszłość innowacyjnego Śląska
text: Dwa dni rozmów i warsztatów były okazją do podsumowania najważniejszych zmian technologicznych mijającego roku, prognozowania trendów na 2027 rok oraz rozmowy o roli Śląska w budowaniu innowacyjnej gospodarki. Choć konferencja rozpoczęła się uroczystym panelem, godzinę przed nim uczestnicy mogli wziąć udział w speed datingu. Przez 3 minuty każdy z nich miał szansę rozwinąć rozpoczęte rozmowy lub poznać perspektywy osób, z którymi jeszcze nie zdążył porozmawiać. Tematy dotyczyły nie tylko AI i biznesu, ale miały także regionalny charakter, o którym wspominali później otwierający konferencję prowadzący. Bardzo się cieszę, że kolejny raz organizujemy InfoShare Katowice; edycję, podczas której mocno skupiamy się na technologii, podsumowujemy rok i patrzymy w przyszłość. Ten format żyje i się rozwija. W tym roku mamy ponad 1000 uczestników i bardzo inspirującą agendę. Mam też nadzieję, że to, o czym dyskutujemy w Katowicach, znajdzie swoją kontynuację także podczas naszej flagowej konferencji w maju przyszłego roku w Gdańsku - powiedział Grzegorz Borowski, pomysłodawca i organizator InfoShare. Podczas ceremonii otwarcia głos zabrali przedstawiciele administracji publicznej, których obecność podkreślała znaczenie współpracy międzysektorowej w budowaniu przyszłości technologicznej regionu. Waldemar Bojarun, członek Zarządu Województwa Śląskiego, mówił o szansach, jakie IV rewolucja przemysłowa w postaci AI daje przedsiębiorstwom. Bogumił Sobula, wiceprezydent Miasta Katowice, podkreślił potrzebę zadbania o bezpieczeństwo nowych narzędzi, a Leszek Pietraszek z Górnośląsko-Zagłębiowskiej Metropolii zwrócił uwagę na rozwój nowoczesnego przemysłu w regionie, w tym także technologii kosmicznych i kwantowych. Na koniec do uczestników Infoshare Katowice przemówił Minister Cyfryzacji Krzysztof Gawkowski, który w nagranej wypowiedzi podkreślił, że Katowice to doskonałe miejsce do rozmowy o transformacji gospodarki, a także zachęcił do dalszych działań na rzecz rozwoju nowych technologii, które coraz częściej odnoszą sukcesy na skalę globalną. Porozmawiajmy o trendach Listopadowe spotkanie pozwoliło spojrzeć na mijający rok z perspektywy doświadczeń nauki, biznesu i sektora technologicznego. Wśród tematów, które szczególnie mocno zaznaczyły swoją obecność, znalazły się sztuczna inteligencja, automatyzacja oraz zmieniające się podejście przedsiębiorstw do cyfrowej transformacji. Rozmowy nie koncentrowały się jednak wyłącznie na nowych rozwiązaniach. Równie istotne było określenie, które z obserwowanych trendów mają szansę przełożyć się na długofalowe zmiany w gospodarce i jakie kompetencje będą potrzebne, by wykorzystać ich potencjał w 2027 roku. Istotnym uzupełnieniem tej perspektywy była rozmowa o odporności biznesu. W wystąpieniu „Odporny biznes. Dron, sabotaż, blackout - jak przygotować firmę na nowe zagrożenia?” Jarosław Stelmach zwrócił uwagę na znaczenie przygotowania organizacji na sytuacje kryzysowe i zagrożenia, które coraz częściej wykraczają poza tradycyjnie rozumiane bezpieczeństwo przedsiębiorstw. Pokazało to, że planowanie przyszłości biznesu wymaga dziś nie tylko inwestowania w innowacje, ale również budowania odporności na nieprzewidywalne zdarzenia. Rozmowy o przyszłości technologii dotyczyły nie tylko sztucznej inteligencji, ale również tego, jak zmieniające się otoczenie wpływa na strategie przedsiębiorstw. Wystąpienie „Przyszłość już tu jest tylko w wersji beta, czyli sygnały zmian 2027”, prowadzone przez Monikę Borycką i Joannę Frotę-Kurkowską, pokazało, że to właśnie umiejętność odpowiednio wczesnego dostrzegania zmian i trendów decyduje o tym, jak firmy przygotują się na kolejne wyzwania rynkowe. Powrót do lokalizmu w biznesie Ta szersza perspektywa prowadziła do kolejnego ważnego wątku konferencji, czyli znaczenia lokalnych ekosystemów i współpracy w rozwoju innowacji. Podczas panelu „Innowacyjny region: jak wspólnie budować ekosystem przyszłości?” Łukasz Żółciak, Mateusz Piech, Kuba Nagórski i Wojciech Maroszek rozmawi

title: Quoting Levent Alpöge
text: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. [...] Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. — Levent Alpöge , alpo.ge/remark.pdf Tags: anthropic , claude , generative-ai , mathematics , ai , llms , levent-alpoge
